newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia rebels set to hand over hostage troops.
newsitem.headline: Colombia rebels set to hand over hostage troops.

text.p: Colombian rebels preparing for a weekend release of 70 captive army troops patrolled their demilitarized zone on Friday on alert for any possible military attack.

The hostage handover, set for Sunday, is a key part of an agreement between the government of President Ernesto Samper and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) that left the rebels in charge of a large swathe of countryside.
Rebel and local leaders on Friday voiced hopes the weekend transfer would go smoothly.

"For the moment there's an agreement (for the army to stay out of the zone) but we mustn't get too confident because then the military will attack us," a guerrilla known as "William" said at a rebel checkpoint just outside this town in the heart of Caqueta province. "The army could come in at any time and so we have been told to remain mobile," he added.

Samper ordered 5,000 army troops to pull out of a 5,000 square mile (13,000 sq km) area of Caqueta this month for 32 days to allow the FARC to release 60 soldiers and 10 marines it has been holding prisoner for as long as nine months.
Their capture and subsequent demilitarization of the area is one of the biggest strategic victories for the FARC, Latin America's largest and oldest guerrilla army, set up in 1964.

Cartagena del Chaira is the heart of a vast coca-growing region known as the Caguan, part of the 50 percent of Colombia analysts say is under guerrilla control. Mayor Victor Oime has declared a "Day for Peace, Liberty, Work and the Environment" and on Friday he said he hoped the handover might lead to a lasting understanding between the rebels and the military.
Like most Colombians who are tired of an internal conflict that has been raging for more than three decades, Oime wants peace but said it must include social justice.
"We need a peace with solutions, a peace with public works programmes. Peace must go hand-in-hand with ideas about how to generate jobs and well-being," he said.

Rebel William, however, said he doubted the troop handover will open the way to broader peace negotiations. "Peace would be good for the country but at the moment I don't think it is possible to reach any kind of agreement," he said.
